questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a simplified model gives up
questions.learningObjective: say what a deliberately simplified model has discarded
questions.stem: A team replaces a real help desk with a model in which every customer is identical and every case takes exactly the average time. What has that model deliberately given up?

options.text: The spread of the case times and the differences between customers, keeping only the average
Nothing that matters, because an average case already carries the whole picture of a desk
options.misconception: believes an average is a complete substitute for the variation it replaced

options.text: Only the customer names, since the spread of the case times is still represented exactly
options.misconception: thinks averaging a duration still preserves how spread out the durations were

options.text: The arrival rate itself, since a model is free to pick whatever input rate suits it
options.misconception: believes a model supplies its own inputs rather than being fed them

questions.explanation: A simplification is a bargain, and the terms of it are always the same: whatever the model smooths away is the thing it can no longer tell you about. Replacing a spread of case times with their mean means every case in the model takes the same time, so the model can say how long the average case takes and nothing about which cases are the long ones. That matters because queues are made entirely of the variation: a desk with a mean of twenty minutes and a spread from two minutes to two hours behaves nothing like a desk with a steady twenty minutes. The test of a simplification is not whether it is defensible but whether the detail it dropped could ever have changed the answer being asked of it.
questions.hint: Ask which numbers the model can no longer produce after the averaging, and whether queues depend on those numbers.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Spread a single parameter cannot hold
questions.learningObjective: compute the spread a one-parameter model removes
questions.stem: A model replaces twenty measured service times with one parameter set to their mean. The twenty times sum to 160 minutes, the shortest is 4 minutes and the longest is 15 minutes. How many minutes of spread does that single parameter hide?
questions.explanation: The mean is 160 divided by 20, which is 8 minutes, so the model places every case at 8. The distance from 8 down to the shortest case is 4 minutes and the distance from 8 up to the longest is 7 minutes, and together they are 11 minutes of spread the model cannot represent. The same 11 falls straight out of the range, since the longest case is 15 and the shortest is 4. The point of the number is that a single parameter can reproduce the centre of a distribution but not its width, and any question whose answer depends on how variable the times are is a question the model has been built to be unable to answer.
questions.hint: Compare the mean with the shortest and with the longest time, or simply take the difference between the two extremes.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reading the error of a simplified model
questions.learningObjective: compute a mean absolute error from a prediction table
questions.stem: A simplified model predicts a demand figure for five days: 12.0, 15.0, 9.0, 18.0 and 14.0. The figures actually recorded on those days were 12, 16, 6, 22 and 13. What is the model's mean absolute error over the five days?

options.text: 1.8, since the gaps are 0, 1, 3, 4 and 1 and they total 9 over 5 days
0.2, since the signed gaps cancel down to 1 and 1 over 5 is the average error
options.misconception: adds signed gaps so that over- and under-predictions cancel

options.text: 4.0, since the largest single gap is the figure a reader would notice
options.misconception: reports the worst single day as though it were the average error

options.text: 0.0, because two of the five days matched exactly and the rest were close to them
options.misconception: believes matching days cancel the days that did not match

questions.explanation: The gaps between prediction and record are 0, 1, 3, 4 and 1, and absolute error means none of them are allowed to cancel, so they total 9 and the mean is 9 over 5, which is 1.8. The signed total does come to 1, giving 0.2, but that number says only that the model over-predicted as often as it under-predicted by about the same amount; on the day it predicted 9 against a real 6 and the day it predicted 18 against a real 22, it was wrong by 3 and 4 while looking fine on average. Averaging signed errors is exactly what a simplified model is tempted to do, because the cancellation flatters it, and it is the reason mean absolute error is the measure used here.
questions.hint: Take the size of each gap before adding, because an error has a direction but no sign.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Fitting a straight line by least squares
questions.learningObjective: compute the least-squares slope of a fitted line
questions.stem: Four observations are recorded: at t = 1 the reading is 3, at t = 2 it is 5, at t = 3 it is 8, and at t = 4 it is 10. A straight line is fitted to the four points by least squares. What is the fitted slope?
questions.explanation: The mean of t is 2.5 and the mean of the readings is 6.5. Subtracting each mean from its value and multiplying the pairs gives 5.25, 0.75, 0.75 and 5.25, which total 12, while the squared deviations of t alone total 5, so the slope is 12 over 5, which is 2.4. The intercept then falls out of the means at 0.5, and the fitted line reads 2.9, 5.3, 7.7 and 10.1, leaving residuals of 0.1, minus 0.3, 0.3 and minus 0.1. The line misses every point on purpose, because least squares minimises the total squared miss rather than insisting on hitting any of them.
questions.hint: Subtract each mean from each value, multiply the pairs and add, then divide by the spread of the t values on their own.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reading a fit beyond its fitted range
questions.learningObjective: explain what changes when a fit is used outside the data it was fitted on
questions.stem: A straight line was fitted by least squares to readings taken between t = 1 and t = 4, and it is now being used to predict at t = 7, which no reading has ever reached. What is the status of that prediction?

options.text: Outside every point the fit saw, so the line is being trusted well beyond the range that fixed it
Inside the confidence of the fit, because a straight line keeps holding however far it is read
options.misconception: believes a fitted form stays trustworthy at any distance

options.text: Already measured, since the fitted line reports a value at any t a reader asks about
options.misconception: confuses what a formula can compute with what has been observed

options.text: An average of two fitted readings, because t = 7 lies midway between t = 4 and t = 10
options.misconception: believes a line prediction is always an average of nearby points

questions.explanation: A fit is fixed by the data that constrained it, and between t = 1 and t = 4 the readings pull the line into a particular place and slope. Past t = 4 nothing pulls it at all, so it is free to keep going in whatever direction its slope happened to take, and the further out the read the more the answer is being set by the shape of the model rather than by evidence. Nothing about the arithmetic changes and everything about the warrant does. The honest description of the t = 7 figure is therefore a projection of the fitted line, and a projection is worth exactly as much as the assumption that the relationship keeps its form beyond the last observation, which is an assumption and not a finding.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence exists on the far side of t = 4 to hold the line in the position the fit gave it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Projecting a fitted line forward
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a fitted line at a point outside the observed range
questions.stem: A straight line is fitted by least squares to the four points (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 8) and (4, 10), giving a slope of 2.4 and an intercept of 0.5. The line is then used to predict at t = 6. What value does it return?
questions.explanation: Substituting t = 6 into 0.5 + 2.4t gives 0.5 + 14.4, which is 14.9, and the same figure comes from adding 2.4 twice to the fitted value at t = 4, which was 10.1. The number is arithmetically unarguable and evidentially hollow: the largest t anyone observed is 4, so t = 6 is half a span of pure projection, and the gap between this answer and the last real reading of 10 is 4.9, which the model produced without a single observation to support it. Recording the fitted value at the edge of the data next to any projected value is what lets a reader see how much of the answer is arithmetic and how much is faith.
questions.hint: Multiply the slope by 6, add the intercept, and remember the answer sits outside the data.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A parameter that has to be measured
questions.learningObjective: identify which model parameters must be estimated from data
questions.stem: A queueing model needs one number for the mean time a case is handled, and the team holds 400 finished cases with recorded handling times. Where must that number come from?

options.text: From the recorded times themselves, since only measurements can estimate a rate nobody has stated
From a published average for the trade, since a desk's own times cannot be summarised
options.misconception: believes a borrowed industry average is a valid substitute for measurement

options.text: From the number of cases handled per day, since a count is itself a direct measure of duration
options.misconception: treats a count of completions as though it measured how long each took

options.text: From the number of staff on shift, since staffing is what sets the time a case takes
options.misconception: believes headcount determines the mean handling time

questions.explanation: A parameter is a number the model cannot run without, and if the real world has not been asked for it then it has to be estimated from whatever the world did record. The 400 handling times are exactly the right evidence, because the mean of them is an estimate of the desk's own mean rather than of some other desk's. Staffing and daily counts are related to the handling time but neither is it, and a published average imports another organisation's process along with its number, which is defensible only as a starting guess and never as a fitted value. The general rule is blunt: a parameter that describes this system must come from this system, and a number typed in from outside is an assumption wearing a model's clothes.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four sources actually measured how long cases took in this particular place.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Estimating an arrival rate from a log
questions.learningObjective: compute an arrival rate in consistent units from counts and hours
questions.stem: A support counter logged 233 arrivals during the 5.5 hours it was open on one day. The model needs the arrival rate expressed in arrivals per hour. What rate do the records give?
questions.explanation: The rate is the count divided by the time it was counted over, so 233 arrivals over 5.5 hours is 42.3636, which rounds to 42.4 arrivals per hour. Multiplying both sides by ten to clear the half gives 2330 over 55, and that division lands on the same 42.3636, which is the check that the units have not been flipped. Keeping the units honest is the whole difficulty here: 233 is an impressive number that means nothing at all until it is divided by the hours it refers to, and a model fed 233 as its rate will be running roughly five and a half times too fast and will over-predict every queue it touches.
questions.hint: Divide the number of arrivals by the number of hours, and keep the answer in arrivals per hour.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Giving each parameter a defensible source
questions.learningObjective: pair a parameter with the measurement that estimates it
questions.stem: A team must set two numbers in a model of a repair shop: the mean time a repair takes and the rate at which jobs arrive. Which pairing gives each number a source that can be defended?

options.text: Mean repair time from 300 completed jobs; arrival rate from counting arrivals in 40 logged hours
Mean repair time from the shop's own quote to customers; arrival rate from the bays it has fitted out
options.misconception: believes a price quote and a bay count are measurements of time and rate

options.text: Mean repair time from the longest job ever seen; arrival rate from the busiest single hour
options.misconception: uses extremes as though they estimated an average

options.text: Mean repair time from a trade average; arrival rate from how many staff are rostered
options.misconception: borrows both numbers from outside the shop being modelled

questions.explanation: A parameter is estimated by the procedure that measures the thing it stands for, and both numbers in the first pair come from records of the shop itself over a decent stretch of time, which is what turns a guess into an estimate with a spread around it. The other pairs all reach for a number that is adjacent to the parameter without being it: a quote is what a customer is charged rather than what a job occupies a bay for, a bay count is a capacity rather than a flow, the longest job and the busiest hour are the extreme tails rather than the centres, and a trade average describes a different shop. The failure is always the same, namely substituting something easy to count for the thing the model actually needs.
questions.hint: Ask of each number whether it was measured on this shop, over a period of time, as an average or a count per hour.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How many observations a fit needs
questions.learningObjective: state the number of observations needed to determine a set of parameters
questions.stem: A model has four free parameters and is fitted by least squares, which succeeds only when the observations pull on all four in independent directions. What is the smallest number of observations that can pull on all four?
questions.explanation: Least squares builds a square matrix with one row and column per parameter and solves it for the values, and that matrix comes out invertible only when the observations span every parameter direction separately, which needs at least as many observations as there are parameters. With three observations the fourth parameter can be raised while a third is lowered in just the right proportion and the fit to the data does not move at all, so the fit returns one member of a whole family of answers and picks among them by a tie-break rule rather than by evidence. Four observations is the floor, not a comfortable number, and in practice teams fit far more than the floor precisely because a fit that just clears it has no room left to be wrong in an interesting way.
questions.hint: Count the unknowns the fit has to solve for, then consider what one fewer observation leaves free to move.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Two parameter sets, one output
questions.learningObjective: name the situation where data cannot separate two parameter sets
questions.stem: Two different sets of parameter values make a model produce exactly the same output for every input in the range that was tested. What is that situation called?

options.text: Non-identifiability, because the data cannot tell the two parameter sets apart
Redundancy, because the two sets are duplicates that should have been dropped before fitting
options.misconception: believes identical fits mean duplicate data rows

options.text: Overfitting, because a model giving more than one answer to the same data has too many parameters
options.misconception: confuses an undetermined fit with one that has too many parameters

options.text: Convergence, because the fit settled on values it could no longer improve on
options.misconception: equates two equally good fits with a fitting process that has settled

questions.explanation: Identifiability asks whether the data can single out one parameter set from all the sets that would have fitted equally well, and when several do, the model as written is non-identifiable. This is not a numerical accident that more careful arithmetic would fix, it is a property of the form: a model with two parameters that only ever appear as their product can trade them against each other for ever without the predicted values shifting by a rounding error. The practical consequence is severe, because a non-identifiable parameter can wander to an absurd value that the fit is perfectly happy with, and a model whose time horizon is a free parameter can be made to predict anything. Fixing it means changing the model or the data, never improving the solver.
questions.hint: Ask whether the data could ever distinguish the two sets, and whether the failure is arithmetic or structural.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Counting the parameters the data leave free
questions.learningObjective: count undetermined parameters from equations and unknowns
questions.stem: A model of the form y = a + b x + c x squared is fitted to two observations only: y = 3 at x = 1 and y = 7 at x = 3. How many of the three parameters does the data leave undetermined?

options.text: One, because two observations give two equations for three unknowns and the third slides freely
None, because a fit is always able to solve for every parameter it was given
options.misconception: assumes a fit succeeds whenever it is allowed to start

options.text: Two, because only the first observation can be trusted in a fit this small
options.misconception: discards a data point instead of counting the equations it supplies

options.text: Three, because no pair of observations pins down a value at any point in between
options.misconception: believes under-determination leaves every parameter free

questions.explanation: Two observations give the equations a + b + c = 3 and a + 3b + 9c = 7. Subtracting the first from the second leaves 2b + 8c = 4, so b is 2 minus 4c, and putting that back into the first equation gives a as 1 plus 3c. Every value of c therefore produces a triple that fits both points exactly: c = 0 gives (1, 2, 0), c = 1 gives (4, -2, 1) and c = -2 gives (-5, 10, -2), all of which reproduce 3 at x = 1 and 7 at x = 3. One parameter is pinned by the arithmetic and one is free, and a fit that reports all three as if it had measured them is reporting a tie-break as though it were a result.
questions.hint: Write the two equations, subtract one from the other, and see how many unknowns still move when you change one of them.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The error a flexible fit drives to zero
questions.learningObjective: compare residual error for a simple and a saturated fit
questions.stem: Five observations at t = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 have values 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15. A straight line is fitted to them, and then a second model with five free parameters is fitted to the same five points. By how much does the sum of squared residuals fall?
questions.explanation: The straight line has slope 35 over 10, which is 3.5, and an intercept of 0, so it predicts 0, 3.5, 7, 10.5 and 14. The residuals are 1, minus 0.5, minus 1, minus 0.5 and 1, and their squares add to 1 + 0.25 + 1 + 0.25 + 1, which is 3.5; the same figure follows from the total spread of the values, 126, minus 3.5 times the co-variation of 35. A model with five free parameters has as many parameters as there are points, so it can pass through every one of them and its residual sum of squares is zero. The whole 3.5 is therefore bought with parameters rather than with skill, which is exactly the trade that has to be judged on cases the fit never saw.
questions.hint: Fit the line, square and add its residuals, then compare that with the error a model can reach when it has as many parameters as points.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reading the symptom of overfitting
questions.learningObjective: diagnose overfitting from the gap between fitted and unseen error
questions.stem: A model's error on the cases it was fitted to keeps falling as parameters are added, while its error on unseen cases stays high or rises. What does that pattern tell you?

options.text: It has memorised the fitted cases, so the extra parameters bought fitted-data error and no general skill
It has improved, because a smaller error on the fitted cases is the clearest measure of quality
options.misconception: treats fitted-data error as the measure of a model's worth

options.text: It needs more parameters still, since the unseen error will fall once the fitting is finished
options.misconception: assumes unseen error is delayed rather than damaged by added parameters

options.text: It has generalised well, because a gap between the two errors is what a well-built model shows
options.misconception: reads a widening gap as evidence of generalisation

questions.explanation: The two errors measure different things and only one of them rewards cheating. Error on the fitted cases can always be pushed down, because a model with enough freedom can be bent until it passes through every point it was shown, and doing that tells you nothing about a case it has not met. Error on unseen cases is the only one that is measured under the same conditions the model will actually meet, and when it stops falling while the first keeps dropping, the parameters being added are being spent on memorising noise in the fitted sample. The gap between the two is the diagnostic, and a gap that widens as a model is refined is the clearest available evidence that the refinement has gone too far.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two error figures can be reduced by memorising, and which is measured on cases the model has not seen.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Choosing between fits on unseen error
questions.learningObjective: select a model using unseen-case error rather than fitted-case error
questions.stem: Three models are scored on the cases they were fitted to and then on a fresh batch. Model A scores 0.4 then 0.5, model B scores 0.1 then 1.8, and model C scores 0.3 then 0.4. Which model should be deployed, and what is the gap between its two scores?

options.text: Model A, with a gap of 0.1, because it is the only one whose fresh score is not the lowest
options.misconception: picks a model on a small gap while ignoring its worse fresh score

options.text: Model B, with a gap of 1.7, because its low fitted score is the strongest evidence available
options.misconception: ranks models by the score they achieved on their own fitted cases

options.text: Model C, with a gap of 0.1, because it has the lowest fresh score and a small gap
Model C, with a gap of 0.7, because the size of the gap is the deciding figure on its own
options.misconception: believes the gap matters more than the fresh score itself

questions.explanation: The fresh batch is the only column measured on cases the models had not seen, and there model C scores 0.4 against A's 0.5 and B's 1.8, so C is the one to deploy. The gap then says whether the fitted score was honest, and C's gap of 0.1 is as small as A's, so C leads on both counts and the choice is not a trade-off. B is the instructive case: its fitted score of 0.1 is by far the best number in the table and its fresh score of 1.8 is by far the worst, a 1.7 gap that is the signature of a model bent around the cases it was shown. Note that A carries the same 0.1 gap as C and is still the wrong answer, which is the reason the gap has to be read alongside the fresh score rather than instead of it.
questions.hint: Rank on the fresh score first, then use the gap to check whether the fitted score was telling the truth.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A straight line forced through a curve
questions.learningObjective: compute the residual error left by an underfitted model
questions.stem: Five observations are recorded at t = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 with values 9, 4, 1, 4 and 9. A straight line is fitted to them by least squares. What sum of squared residuals does the fit leave behind?
questions.explanation: The five points are mirror images about t = 2, so each one is as far above the middle as another is below it and the fitted slope comes out at exactly zero. The line is therefore the mean of the values, which is 5.4, and the residuals against it are 3.6, minus 1.4, minus 4.4, minus 1.4 and 3.6. Their squares are 12.96, 1.96, 19.36, 1.96 and 12.96, which total 49.2. Because the slope vanished, that total is also just the spread of the values about their own mean, so 49.2 measures how little a straight line can say about a pattern that rises, falls and rises again. Adding more of the same kind of term cannot help, because no amount of straightness bends.
questions.hint: Check whether the points are symmetric about their middle, because that forces the fitted slope to be zero.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A curved pattern the model cannot bend
questions.learningObjective: diagnose underfitting from a patterned set of residuals
questions.stem: A model's residuals against its fitted values form a smooth curve that is positive at both ends and negative in the middle, and adding more terms of the same kind leaves the error untouched. What is happening, and what does it call for?

options.text: The model is too simple for the pattern; a different family of terms should be tried rather than more of the same
The model is too flexible; more terms of the same kind will absorb the curve and the error will fall
options.misconception: reads a patterned residual curve as evidence that the fit needs more capacity

options.text: The readings are faulty; a smooth curve in the residuals means the values were altered by hand
options.misconception: blames the data for a structure the model form cannot represent

options.text: The fit is sound; a smooth curve in the residuals is what a well-specified model always shows
options.misconception: believes any structured residual pattern is a sign of health

questions.explanation: Residuals that arrange themselves into a smooth curve are not noise, they are the part of the pattern the model has no way to express, and their shape tells you what is missing: positive at the ends and negative in the middle is a curve sitting above a straight line in the middle of the range. Adding further terms of the same family cannot fix it, because a straight line with more measuring points along it is still a straight line, and the fact that the error did not move confirms the diagnosis. The remedy is a change of family, typically a term that can bend, and the reason the check is worth doing is that a patterned residual survives a careless reading as a slightly disappointing score rather than as a structural fault in the model.
questions.hint: Ask what shape the residuals trace, and whether the terms available to the model are capable of producing that shape.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a bent term buys over a straight one
questions.learningObjective: compute the error reduction from adding a term that can bend
questions.stem: Readings taken at t = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 were 0, 1, 4, 9 and 16. A straight line is fitted to them, and then a curve of the form a + b t + c t squared is fitted to the same points. By how much does the sum of squared residuals fall?
questions.explanation: The straight line has slope 40 over 10, which is 4, and an intercept of minus 2, so it predicts minus 2, 2, 6, 10 and 14. The residuals are 2, minus 1, minus 2, minus 1 and 2, whose squares add to 4 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 4, which is 14, and the total spread of the values about their mean of 6 confirms the same figure. The values are exactly t squared, so a fit that is allowed a t squared term returns 0, 1, 4, 9 and 16 and leaves nothing behind. The fall is therefore the whole 14, and it was bought with one extra parameter of the right shape rather than with any amount of extra straightness, which is the whole difference between a model that is too simple and one that is merely too eager.
questions.hint: Fit the line, add up its squared residuals, then check whether the values follow a curved form exactly.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A fit carried to a different setting
questions.learningObjective: explain the risk of a fit whose sample came from one setting only
questions.stem: A model is fitted on 500 cases drawn from one hospital and is then used to prioritise cases at a second hospital with a different case mix. What risk has been taken?

options.text: The fitted cases were not drawn from the setting the model now runs in, so its errors there are unmeasured
None, because averaging over 500 cases makes a fit representative of every case that exists
options.misconception: believes a large sample removes the problem of the wrong sample

options.text: Only a small one, because two hospitals share one process even when their case mixes differ
options.misconception: assumes a shared underlying process makes case mix irrelevant

options.text: The second hospital must refit it, but the first hospital's own fit remains valid there
options.misconception: treats a fit as permanently attached to the site that produced it

questions.explanation: A fit learns from the distribution of the cases it was shown, and every coefficient in it encodes something about that distribution, so carrying it to a different case mix imports those assumptions unexamined. Five hundred cases make the estimated parameters precise, which is a different property from making them appropriate, and precision about the wrong population is the most dangerous state a model can be in because it carries its confidence with it. The tell is that nobody has measured the model's error in the new setting, so there is no number to appeal to when the prioritisations start looking wrong. Checking a handful of cases from the new setting against the model's own answers is cheap, and it converts an unknown into a figure that can be acted on.
questions.hint: Ask what the model was shown, and whether anyone has scored it on the cases it is now being used for.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Error measured where the model will be used
questions.learningObjective: compute error on a new sample and contrast it with fitted-case error
questions.stem: A model fitted on 20 cases from last quarter had a mean absolute error of 1.2. It is now used on five new cases, where it predicts 45, 47, 49, 46 and 48 while the real values are 38, 39, 44, 41 and 50. What is its mean absolute error on the new cases?
questions.explanation: The gaps between prediction and reality are 7, 8, 5, 5 and 2, and none of them is allowed to cancel another, so they total 27 and the mean is 27 over 5, which is 5.4. Set against 1.2 on the cases the model was fitted to, that is more than four times the error, and the shape of the gaps is the informative part: the model runs high by 5 to 8 on four of the five cases and low by 2 on the fifth, which is a consistent bias rather than scatter. A consistent bias on new cases is what a fit carried into a shifted case mix looks like, and the fix is not more fitting on the old data but either new data from the setting being served or a deliberate adjustment of the offset.
questions.hint: Work out the gap on each of the five new cases, add the sizes together, and divide by five.

questions.topic: New cases in a band the fit never saw
questions.learningObjective: read off the share of cases falling outside a fitted range
questions.stem: A model was fitted where the input ranged from 0 to 10. In a later quarter the input ranged from 0 to 40, split into four bands. The fitted cases held 18 in the 0 to 10 band and 2 in the 11 to 20 band, with none above 20. The new cases number 2, 3, 6 and 9 in those same four bands. What share of the new cases sit in a band the fitted cases never reached?

options.text: 75 percent, since 15 of the 20 new cases sit in the two bands that held no fitted cases
50 percent, since only the 31 to 40 band is new and it holds 9 of the 20 cases
options.misconception: counts only the single most extreme band as outside the fitted range

options.text: 90 percent, since almost every new case lies beyond what the model was fitted on
options.misconception: estimates the share by impression rather than by adding the counts

options.text: 30 percent, since 6 of the 20 new cases sit in the 21 to 30 band on its own
options.misconception: counts one band as though it were the whole of the unseen range

questions.explanation: The fitted cases reached only as far as the 20 band, so the 21 to 30 and 31 to 40 bands are both new territory, and they hold 6 and 9 new cases, which is 15 of the 20 new cases. Three quarters of the traffic the model now serves comes from a part of the input range where it was never shown a single case, and the remaining quarter is the part it was fitted on. The number is the reason a fitted-case error of 1.2 in the previous quarter told the team nothing about what to expect now: the 1.2 was measured entirely on the quarter of the traffic that still looks familiar, and three quarters of the answer is coming from extrapolation.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The holdout that stopped being held out
questions.learningObjective: explain how reusing a holdout turns it into fitted data
questions.stem: A team tries forty settings for a model, scores every one of them on the same fifty held-back cases, then reports the winner's score on those fifty cases as its honest accuracy. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The fifty cases were used to choose the model, so the winner's score on them is a fitted score
Nothing, because holding cases back is what makes a score honest, however many tries were made
options.misconception: believes any held-back score stays honest however often it is consulted

options.text: Only the wording is loose, since the winner would score the same on any fresh fifty cases
options.misconception: assumes the winning setting would score alike on any fresh sample

options.text: The model is sound but the cases are too few, since forty settings on fifty cases is always too little data
options.misconception: blames the sample size rather than the repeated use of the sample

questions.explanation: Holding cases back protects them only for as long as they are held back. The moment the team compares forty settings on the same fifty cases and keeps the best, the fifty cases have been fitted, and the winner's score on them now measures how well the winner fits those particular cases rather than how well it will do on the next fifty. The inflation is not subtle: it is the same gap between fitted-case and unseen-case error that makes an over-parameterised model look excellent, applied here to a sample of fifty that has been searched forty times over. The number is still an upper bound on real performance, which is a genuine use, but reporting it as an honest estimate is claiming that a search left no trace, and a search always leaves one.
questions.hint: Ask what the fifty cases were used for, and whether the reported score was still measured on cases that had played no part.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How far the best of many tries overshoots
questions.learningObjective: estimate the inflation in a best-of-many score
questions.stem: Forty candidate settings are each scored on the same holdout, and the scores are spread around 0.70 with a standard deviation of 0.05. The team reports the best of the forty rather than a typical one. On average, what score does the best of the forty reach?
questions.explanation: The best of forty draws does not land at the average, it lands roughly 2.16 standard deviations above it, so 0.70 plus 0.05 times 2.16 gives 0.808. That figure is confirmed twice over: a simulation of 200,000 independent batches of forty draws returns 0.8081, and numerical integration of the density of the largest of forty draws returns 0.8080. The gap between 0.808 and the true 0.70, a little over 0.10, is the whole cost of reporting a best-of-many figure, and it grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the number of tries, which is why forty looks modest and behaves badly. The cure is not fewer tries but a holdout the search never touched.
questions.hint: The best of many draws sits further above the mean the more draws are taken, and for forty that is about 2.16 standard deviations.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Two teams, two reports, one honest number
questions.learningObjective: judge which reported accuracy can be trusted and why
questions.stem: Two teams both report 91 percent accuracy. Team A tried six settings on 400 cases and then scored the winner on 200 untouched cases. Team B tried six settings on 200 cases and then reported the best score from those same 200. Which report is the safer number, and on what grounds?

options.text: Team A's, because its final score came from cases that played no part in choosing the setting
Team B's, because scoring on the tuning cases puts the model under a harder test than fresh cases would
options.misconception: believes a score on reused cases is a stricter rather than a rosier test

options.text: Neither, because both teams tried six settings and the number of tries is what inflates a score
options.misconception: treats the number of attempts as the whole story, ignoring what was set aside

options.text: Team A's, because 400 cases is twice what Team B used and the sample size is what decides it
options.misconception: attributes trustworthiness to sample size rather than to independence

questions.explanation: Both teams report the same figure from the same number of cases, so neither the number nor the count distinguishes them, and what separates them is whether the final score was measured on cases that had played no part in choosing the setting. Team A's 200 untouched cases did exactly that, so its 91 percent is an estimate of performance on the next 200 cases. Team B's 200 cases chose the setting and then scored it, so its 91 percent is the best of six figures drawn from a sample of that size and is biased upwards, and the bias grows with the number of tries. Option D is the trap worth naming, because doubling the sample does make the estimate steadier without making it any less biased.
questions.hint: Ask of each team's final number whether the cases behind it were used to choose the model or only to score it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: An input that only exists after the answer
questions.learningObjective: recognise leakage from an input unavailable at prediction time
questions.stem: A model predicts whether a repair will overrun its budget. It is trained on finished jobs and one of its inputs is how many status emails the job had already generated. What is wrong with that input?

options.text: It can only be counted once the job is over, so the model learns from something absent when it must predict
Nothing, because the emails are in the job file and the file is available to the model at run time
options.misconception: treats availability in the archive as availability at prediction time

options.text: Only the volume matters, so counting emails from a fixed window before the deadline is just as valid
options.misconception: believes narrowing the window removes the availability problem

options.text: It is a weak predictor rather than an unfair one, since a weak input is still a legitimate input
options.misconception: reduces leakage to the question of how predictive the input is

questions.explanation: The test for a legitimate input is not whether it predicts well but whether it exists at the moment the prediction is required, and the email count only reaches its final figure once the job has closed, which is after the answer the model was supposed to supply. Trained on finished jobs, the model discovers that long-running jobs generate many emails, so the input carries the answer in its own total rather than any early signal of it, and the fitted score is inflated by an amount that will not be there in production. This is leakage, and the tell is always the same: a score that collapses on fresh data taken at the real prediction moment, which is why the freshness of the evaluation data matters as much as the honesty of the features.
questions.hint: Ask at what moment the number is known, and compare that with the moment the model has to produce its answer.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Two scores from one set of cases
questions.learningObjective: use the collapse of a fresh score to identify a leaky input
questions.stem: Two models are scored on the same 200 finished jobs. Model A uses only inputs known when a job is booked and scores 0.78 on the cases used for tuning and 0.76 on a fresh batch. Model B adds one input, the number of status emails already sent, and scores 0.97 on the tuning cases and 0.65 on the fresh batch. Which model should be deployed?

options.text: Model A, since its fresh score holds at 0.76 while B's falls from 0.97 all the way to 0.65
Model B, since 0.97 on 200 cases is far stronger evidence of quality than A's 0.78 on them
options.misconception: judges a model on its score on the cases used to tune it

options.text: Model A, since B's extra input leaves its fresh score 0.11 below A's on the same cases
options.misconception: reaches the right choice while claiming the extra input is simply a weaker signal

options.text: Model B, since it carries one more input and more inputs always sharpen a model's predictions
options.misconception: believes the number of inputs is itself a sign of a better model

questions.explanation: A's two scores are 0.78 and 0.76, a gap of 0.02, so its tuning figure has been honest and it is performing at 0.76 on cases it had not been tuned on. B's two scores are 0.97 and 0.65, a gap of 0.32 in the wrong direction, and the fresh batch of 0.65 is below A's 0.76 on the same jobs, so the extra input made the model worse at the job it will actually do. The 0.97 was never a measure of the model's skill: it was a measure of how well the email count, which only fills up as a job overruns, describes jobs that have already overrun. Option C names the right model for the wrong reason, and its error is worth naming too, since calling leakage a weak signal is what lets the input stay in the model.
questions.hint: Compare each model's two scores, and ask whether the fresh batch was measured at the moment a real prediction is made.

questions.topic: Counting the cases only the leaky input got right
questions.learningObjective: convert two scores into a count of cases won by leakage
questions.stem: A model is fitted on 200 finished jobs and scores 0.97 on them. When the input that can only be known once a job has closed is removed, the same model scores 0.78 on the same 200 jobs. How many of those 200 jobs were classified correctly only because that input was there?
questions.explanation: A score of 0.97 on 200 jobs is 194 correct and a score of 0.78 on them is 156, and 194 minus 156 is 38. The same 38 comes from the difference of the two scores, 0.19, multiplied by 200. Those 38 jobs are the ones the model could only get right by reading a total that had not been reached when the prediction was due, so in production they would have arrived with whatever the model decided without it and roughly a fifth of its correct answers would disappear. Quoting a difference of scores rather than a count of cases is the easy way to miss how large the problem is: nineteen percent of a model's apparent skill is not a rounding matter.
questions.hint: Turn each score into a number of correct jobs out of 200, then subtract one count from the other.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A second influence riding along with the first
questions.learningObjective: identify a confounder and the effect of ignoring it
questions.stem: A study finds that patients given a new treatment recover faster, and it turns out that nearly all the treated patients were treated at one hospital whose case mix differs from the hospital where the untreated patients were treated. What is the extra influence at work?

options.text: The hospital itself, so part or all of the difference in recovery may be a difference between case mixes
Nothing, because the difference in recovery was measured rather than estimated and is immune to it
options.misconception: believes a measured difference cannot be produced by a confounder

options.text: Only sample size, since a small study mixes the hospitals together and a large one separates them
options.misconception: believes a confounder is removed automatically by gathering more cases

options.text: A random effect, since patients chose their hospital and so no adjustment is possible
options.misconception: treats a patient's own choice as a barrier to adjusting for the hospital

questions.explanation: A confounder is a second influence that travels with the first and can produce the whole of an apparent effect, and here the hospital is it: the treated group and one hospital are almost the same set of patients, so any difference between the hospitals in how sick their patients were will appear as a difference attributed to the treatment. The reason it is dangerous is that the two influences are not merely correlated but nearly inseparable in the data, which means no amount of extra data collected the same way will separate them. The cure is structural rather than numerical, namely comparing like with like by comparing the two treatments within the same hospital, so the hospital stops varying while the treatment varies. Ignoring the confounder does not merely add noise, it can point the conclusion the wrong way.
questions.hint: Ask what else distinguishes the treated patients from the untreated ones apart from the treatment itself.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The verdict a confounder reverses
questions.learningObjective: compute a stratified difference and contrast it with a crude one
questions.stem: A scheme runs in sites A and B but not in sites C and D. Failures run at 45 and 5 per 100 in A and B with the scheme, and at 50 and 10 per 100 in C and D without it. Nine tenths of the scheme cases come from A, and nine tenths of the non-scheme cases come from D. Compared across all cases at once the scheme looks 27 points worse. Compared within each site, by how many points per 100 is it actually better?
questions.explanation: Pooled, the scheme cases give 90 times 45 plus 10 times 5 over 100, which is 41, while the non-scheme cases give 10 times 50 plus 90 times 10 over 100, which is 14, and 41 against 14 is the 27 point penalty the crude comparison reports. Within site A the scheme runs at 45 against 50, and within site B at 5 against 10, so it is 5 points better in each and 5 points better on average across the two sites. The site is the confounder, because the scheme was pushed into the harsher site, and pooling then charges the scheme for the harshness of the site it happened to run in. Ignoring this does not weaken a conclusion, it inverts one.
questions.hint: Compare the scheme against no scheme inside each site first, then average those two differences.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Finding the comparison that reverses a verdict
questions.learningObjective: select the stratified comparison that exposes a confounder
questions.stem: A comparison table lists failures per 100 by site and by whether the scheme ran. Site A: 45 with the scheme, 50 without. Site B: 5 with, 10 without. Nine tenths of the scheme cases came from site A. Which single comparison reverses the crude verdict?

options.text: Comparing the sites separately, where the scheme has 5 fewer failures per 100 inside each of them
Comparing the pooled totals, where the scheme carries 27 more failures per 100 across all cases
options.misconception: keeps the pooled comparison and reads its 27 points as a settled result

options.text: Comparing site A alone, where the scheme has 5 fewer failures per 100 in the harsher site
options.misconception: generalises from the single hardest site to every site

options.text: Comparing the scheme cases alone, where the average of 41 per 100 settles the question
options.misconception: treats one group's own average as a fair comparison against no scheme

questions.explanation: Inside site A the scheme's 45 sits 5 below the 50 seen without it, and inside site B its 5 sits 5 below the 10, so on both sites where a comparison is possible the scheme is ahead, and the crude penalty of 27 points comes entirely from the fact that nine tenths of the scheme cases came from the harsher site. Only the separated comparison can produce a reversal, because it is the one that stops the site and the scheme from varying together. Options C and D show the other failure modes: C generalises a single site without checking whether it holds elsewhere, and D compares a group with itself, which produces a number without producing a comparison at all.
questions.hint: Ask which comparison holds the site fixed while letting the scheme vary, and check it at every site where that is possible.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A strong association that changed its mind
questions.learningObjective: explain what a reversal of sign does to a claimed relationship
questions.stem: Two measures move closely together across eight months of records, and the team concludes that the second drives the first. In the following eight months the same two measures move in opposite directions. What does the reversal establish?

options.text: That the first window's association was not a stable relationship, so it supports no claim about cause
That the second measure reverses its own sign, so the first window must have been read backwards
options.misconception: treats a sign change as the quantity itself changing sign

options.text: That eight months is too short a window, so the pattern will appear once more months are gathered
options.misconception: blames the length of the sample for a change in direction

options.text: That the relationship is real but delayed, so aligning the same months will settle it
options.misconception: assumes a reversal can always be undone by shifting the alignment

questions.explanation: A strong association inside one sample is a statement about that sample, and the cheapest way to find out whether it is a property of the world or a coincidence of the window is to collect a second window and see whether the association survives. Here it does not survive but reverses, which is a much stronger result than a weak second window would have been, because a relationship governed by a stable cause cannot change direction when the cause has not changed. The only conclusion that survives both windows is the weak one: the two moved together strongly for a while. Any claim about the second driving the first has been withdrawn, and the follow-up worth doing is to look for what was different about the two periods rather than to keep the original reading.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true about the world for the same pair of measures to move together and then apart.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Measuring how two series move together
questions.learningObjective: compute a correlation coefficient from paired series
questions.stem: Across eight months one measure takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, and a second measure takes 2, 4, 5, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10 over the same months. What is the correlation coefficient between the two?
questions.explanation: The means of the two series are 4.5 and 5.875, and after subtracting them the products of the deviations come to 13.5625, 4.6875, 1.3125, 0.9375, 0.0625, 1.6875, 7.8125 and 14.4375, which total 44.5. The squared deviations of the first series total 42 and of the second 50.875, so the coefficient is 44.5 divided by the square root of 42 times 50.875, which is 44.5 over 46.2258, giving 0.963. Dividing by the two spreads rather than by one is what keeps the figure between minus one and one, and the reason it is high here is simply that both series rise across the window, which is the first thing to suspect about any strong correlation.
questions.hint: Subtract each series' own mean from its values, multiply the pairs and add, then divide by the square root of the two spreads.

questions.topic: The same two measures, a second window
questions.learningObjective: state what a pair of correlations in two windows licenses
questions.stem: The same two measures are collected over the next eight months, where the second takes the values 5, 4, 6, 3, 5, 2, 4 and 3 against the same 1 to 8 for the first. The correlation is now minus 0.53, where the first window gave 0.96. What does the pair of results license?

options.text: Only that the two moved together strongly in the first window, and nothing about a lasting relationship
That the second measure drives the first, since a reversal always confirms a strong underlying link
options.misconception: reads a sign change as confirmation rather than as a retraction

options.text: That the first window was the anomaly, so the relationship to model is the negative one
options.misconception: promotes one window's result to the truth because it is the later one

options.text: That both results hold, so a real relationship exists and changes sign every eight months
options.misconception: reconciles a reversal by inventing a periodic sign change

questions.explanation: Two windows, two correlations, 0.96 and minus 0.53, and the only thing they jointly support is the claim about the first window, because the second window contradicts it. A coefficient that is high in one period and negative in the next has told you something important, but it is not a smaller version of a relationship, it is the absence of one, and any model fitted to the first window alone is fitted to a window that the second window has already contradicted. questions.hint: Ask what claim about the pair of measures is true in both windows at once, rather than only in one of them.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A fitted formula against a running program
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a model fitted to records from a simulation that generates figures
questions.stem: A colleague calls two things models: a formula fitted to past figures, and a program that runs the same queueing rules against randomly chosen arrivals and service times. Which statement separates the two?

options.text: The formula compresses records into one fixed relationship, while the program generates a new set of figures on each run
The formula is a model and the program is not, because only a formula can be fitted to records
options.misconception: excludes a simulation from the category of models entirely

options.text: Both are models, and the only real difference is that the program takes longer to run than the formula
options.misconception: reduces the distinction to a matter of running time

options.text: The program is a model of the formula, since it exists only to check what the formula predicts
options.misconception: treats a simulation as a check on a fit rather than a model itself

questions.explanation: The two arrive at their numbers by opposite routes. A fitted formula compresses a set of records into a relationship that is fixed the moment the fit is finished, so asking it the same question twice gives the same answer twice, and what varies between the answer and the records is the error the fit could not remove. A simulation carries the rules of a system and generates arrivals and service times afresh on every run, so the same question gives a different answer each time and the spread of answers is a real finding about the system rather than a nuisance. This is why a simulation can report a range where a fit reports a single figure, and why replacing a simulation with a fitted formula quietly throws away exactly the information a queueing question is usually about.
questions.hint: Ask where each one's numbers come from, and whether asking it twice gives the same answer twice.

questions.topic: What a simulated mean actually promises
questions.learningObjective: state what a simulated average does and does not guarantee
questions.stem: A simulation of a proposed clinic layout reports a mean wait of 6 minutes over many runs. Which statement about that figure is defensible?

It is the wait a patient will experience, since a simulated mean is the outcome the layout delivers
options.misconception: reads a simulated average as a promise about an individual case

options.text: It is a lower bound on the wait, because randomness in a simulation can only ever lengthen waits
options.misconception: believes sampling variation has a single direction

options.text: It is what every future run will report, since a fixed layout always produces a fixed mean
options.misconception: believes a fixed model removes the randomness from its own output

The spread around the 6 is not decoration, it is the finding, because a layout whose average is 6 with waits running to 30 and a layout whose waits all fall between 5 and 7 are different designs with the same headline number, and only the first tells anyone whether the clinic is usable. Option C is a confusion worth naming separately: randomness in a simulation pushes in both directions, so a run that reports less than the mean is not evidence that the layout is better than one reporting more.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What each kind of model promises
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference in warrant between a fit and a simulation
questions.stem: Explain the difference in what a fitted formula and a simulation each promise about the system they describe, and say which of the two can report a range rather than a single figure.

answer.exemplar: A fitted formula summarises records that already happened: it commits to one fixed relationship, reproduces its own answer on every use, and its error on past cases is the only error it can quote. A simulation carries the rules of the system forward and generates fresh arrivals and service times on each run, so it commits to a distribution of outcomes rather than one number, and it is the simulation that can report a range. Say which follows from which: the fit is a claim about the past compressed, the simulation is a claim about what the rules produce, and only the second says anything about variation.

questions.explanation: The distinction is about what each kind of model is committed to, and it shows up most clearly in how each one behaves when asked the same question twice. A fitted formula answers identically every time, which is a real strength when the question is what the past looked like, and a real limitation when the question is what will happen, because the single answer has quietly absorbed the variation that the records contained. A simulation answers differently every time, and that variation is not error in the answer but the answer: it is the spread of outcomes the rules permit, and a question about waiting times, queue lengths or failures is usually a question about that spread rather than about its centre. A complete answer therefore names the fit as a compression of records and the simulation as a generator of outcomes, and identifies the simulation as the one able to report a range.
questions.hint: Ask each one where its numbers come from, and what happens if you ask it the same question a second time.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a random simulation is rerun from a fixed start
questions.learningObjective: explain what fixing the random starting value makes possible
questions.stem: A simulation of a queueing system reports a mean wait of 11 minutes on one run and 19 on the next, with no change to the code or the inputs. Why is it rerun with a fixed starting value?

options.text: To hold the random choices constant, so a change in the result can be read as a change in the model
To make the run finish faster, since a fixed start removes the need to generate any randomness
options.misconception: believes a fixed starting value removes the random draws themselves

options.text: To compare two runs directly, since a fixed start makes each run give a different answer
options.misconception: expects a fixed starting value to make runs differ from one another

options.text: To make the reported figure exact, since a fixed start removes the sampling error in the output
options.misconception: believes fixing the starting value eliminates sampling error

questions.explanation: A simulation with a random component produces a different result every run for reasons that have nothing to do with the model, and two figures of 11 and 19 minutes are entirely consistent with a system whose true mean is 15. That is what makes the second run useless as evidence about the first: nothing has been isolated, so the difference between them measures the draw and not the design. Fixing the starting value makes the draws reproducible, so the same run comes out again with the same answer and any change in the answer must have come from a change in the model or its inputs. What a fixed start buys is the ability to attribute a difference, and it is the tool that turns two runs into a comparison. It does not make the answer more accurate, and a run repeated from a fixed start many times over is still sampling.
questions.hint: Ask what the difference between 11 and 19 is currently a measure of, and what a fixed start would remove from it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How far a simulated proportion is from the truth
questions.learningObjective: compute a margin of error for a simulated proportion
questions.stem: A simulation estimates a proportion and reports 0.62 from 400 trials. Using the normal approximation, what is the margin of error around that figure at 95 percent confidence?
questions.explanation: The standard error of a proportion is the square root of the proportion times one minus the proportion divided by the number of trials, and here that is the square root of 0.62 times 0.38 over 400, which is the square root of 0.000589, giving 0.024269. Multiplying by 1.96 for 95 percent confidence gives 0.047568, and using 2 instead gives 0.048539, so the margin is about 0.048 either way. The figure is what tells a reader how much of the answer is the model and how much is the number of trials, and it is why 0.62 from 400 trials is worth quoting as 0.62 plus or minus 0.05 rather than as 0.62 on its own. Nothing about the margin is a criticism of the simulation; it is a statement about how many trials were run.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the proportion times its complement divided by the trials, then multiply by 1.96.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The comparison a fixed start makes legitimate
questions.learningObjective: choose the run pairing that isolates a change in the model
questions.stem: Two versions of a simulation of the same queue differ in one rule about how long a service takes. Which pairing of runs is the one that lets a difference in the results be attributed to that rule?

options.text: Run both from the same fixed starting value, so only the changed rule differs between the results
Run both from different starting values, so a difference is more likely to be the changed rule
options.misconception: believes adding more randomness isolates a single change more reliably

options.text: Run one from a fixed start and one from a fresh draw, so the fixed run is the honest baseline
options.misconception: treats one deterministic run as a trustworthy baseline for a random one

options.text: Run both many times unfixed, so a difference that survives repetition is certainly the rule
options.misconception: believes repeating under random draws isolates a single change by itself

questions.explanation: Attributing a difference requires holding everything else equal, and in a simulation the largest thing to hold equal is the random draw itself, because two unfixed runs of the same model differ for no reason connected to the model at all. Giving both versions the same starting value makes the sequence of arrivals and service draws identical, so the two runs are the same experiment with one rule altered and any difference in the outcomes is produced by that rule. Running them from different starts, as in the second pairing, adds a second source of difference rather than removing one. Running many times unfixed, as in the last, does eventually separate a real effect from the draw, but at far more runs than two matched ones need, and it discards the pairing that makes the mechanism obvious.
questions.hint: Ask what else differs between the two runs apart from the one rule, and how to make that list as short as possible.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: When more trials stop changing the answer
questions.learningObjective: explain what a settled simulated estimate means and how to reach it
questions.stem: A simulation of a queueing system is rerun with more trials and reports a mean wait of 11.2 minutes at 1,000 trials, 11.1 at 10,000 and 11.1 at 100,000. Explain what has happened to the estimate, and say how many trials a run like this needs and how a reader should judge that it has enough.

answer.exemplar: The estimate has stopped moving: 11.2, then 11.1, then 11.1, so the remaining wobble is smaller than the last decimal place and the true mean is being pinned down rather than merely approached. The run needs enough trials that the margin of error is smaller than any difference the run will be used to detect, and the margin shrinks only as the square root of the trial count, so a fourfold increase in trials buys only half the margin. Four times the trials to halve the error is the practical rule a reader should apply before believing that a small difference between two runs is a real one.

questions.explanation: A simulated mean converges because the trial after trial average stops jumping, and the three figures here show exactly that pattern: 11.2 moves to 11.1 and then stays at 11.1, so the estimate is no longer being decided by the draw. Convergence is not the same as accuracy, since a converged figure can still be wrong if the rules it simulated are wrong, and a complete answer should keep those two failures apart. What decides how many trials are enough is the comparison the run will be asked to support, because the margin of error falls only as the square root of the trial count, so moving from 1,000 to 100,000 trials, a hundredfold increase, buys a margin smaller by ten and nothing more. A reader should therefore ask what size of difference the run needs to resolve and check the margin against it before treating two close figures as a real difference.
questions.hint: Ask what changed between the three figures, and what size of difference the run will be used to detect.

questions.topic: Trial count for a target margin
questions.learningObjective: compute the trial count needed for a given margin of error
questions.stem: A simulation must estimate a proportion that could be anywhere near one half, and the team needs it to within 0.02 at 95 percent confidence. Using the normal approximation, what is the smallest number of trials that guarantees this?
questions.explanation: The margin is 1.96 times the square root of the proportion times one minus the proportion divided by the trial count, and the demanding case is the proportion of one half, where the product is a quarter. Setting 1.96 times the square root of 0.25 over n to 0.02 and squaring through gives n as 1.96 squared times 0.25 over 0.0004, which is 0.9604 over 0.0004, so 2401 trials. A direct scan of the trial counts confirms 2401 is the first whose margin is at or below 0.02, with 2400 trials giving 0.0200038, just over the line. The figure is also 49 squared, which is why the margin lands on 0.02 exactly there rather than near it, and the same calculation with a smaller margin shows how quickly the cost rises.
questions.hint: Use the widest possible proportion, since that is the case needing the most trials, then solve the inequality for the count.

questions.topic: Why more trials buy so little precision
questions.learningObjective: compute a margin of error at a stated trial count
questions.stem: A simulation estimates a proportion that is close to one half, at 95 percent confidence. What is the margin of error around its estimate when the run uses 1,600 trials?
questions.explanation: Taking the demanding proportion of one half, the margin is 1.96 times the square root of 0.25 over 1600, which is 1.96 times 0.0125, giving 0.0245. The same figure follows from the ratio: 400 trials give a margin of 0.049, and 1,600 is four times as many, so the margin is 0.049 divided by 2, which is 0.0245. That halving for a fourfold increase in trials is the whole practical lesson here, because the square root in the denominator means precision is expensive, and a team wanting twice the precision has to run four times the work rather than twice.
questions.hint: Take the widest proportion, divide the square root of it by the square root of the trials, then multiply by 1.96.

One customer waiting and one in service, because the second has not yet begun to be served
options.misconception: reads the state before the minute 3 event has been applied

options.text: Two customers waiting and none in service, because the server clears both customers at once
options.misconception: believes a single server can finish two services simultaneously

options.text: None waiting and none in service, because the server stands idle in the gap between jobs
options.misconception: confuses the idle gap later in the run with the state at minute 3

questions.explanation: The first customer arrives at minute 1 and occupies the server until minute 3, the second arrives at minute 2, waits that one minute, and is served from minute 3 to minute 4, and the third arrives at minute 5 and is served from minute 5 to minute 8. At minute 3 a departure and a start are the same event, so immediately afterwards one customer is in service and the waiting line is empty. questions.learningObjective: pair a state variable with the decision it supports
questions.stem: A discrete event model of a support desk carries several values forward from one event to the next. Which pairing names a state variable and the decision it is actually used for?

Total cases handled today, used to decide how long each individual case took to handle
options.misconception: treats a running daily total as a measure of one case's duration

options.text: Clock time of day, used to decide how many cases are waiting to be picked up now
options.misconception: believes the time of day reports how busy the desk is

options.text: Staff on shift this hour, used to decide how long the next arriving case will wait
options.misconception: treats a staffing figure as something the model maintains rather than reads

The other three pair a number with a use it cannot support, and the failure in each is the same. questions.topic: Naming and catching an extrapolation error
questions.learningObjective: pair the risk of a projected value with a check that detects it
questions.stem: A model fitted on values of x from 1 to 4 is used to predict the value at x = 6. Which pairing names the risk in that prediction and the check that would catch it going wrong?

options.text: Extrapolation past the fitted range; obtain one real reading near x = 6 and compare it with the prediction
An unlucky random start inside the fitting; refit from a different start and see if the value moves
options.misconception: assumes the fitting itself carries a random start that could be unlucky

options.text: A mis-stated unit on the x axis; convert every x to one common unit and refit before trusting it
options.misconception: treats a unit mismatch as the likeliest reason for a projected value to be wrong

options.text: Too few observations inside the fitted range; gather more values from x = 1 to x = 4 and refit again
options.misconception: believes more data inside the range would check a value outside it

questions.explanation: The risk is that the prediction at x = 6 rests on nothing at all, because the four readings that fixed the line all sit at or below x = 4, and the only check that addresses this is one taken at the place being predicted. A single real reading near x = 6 does not prove the projection right, but it exposes it immediately if the relationship has turned over, and it is far cheaper than discovering the problem after the decision has been acted on. The last option is the trap worth naming, because adding data inside the fitted range does tighten the line without ever touching the question of whether the line continues, and the second misplaces the randomness, which belongs to a simulation rather than to a least-squares fit.

questions.stem: A single-server queue is simulated over a ten-minute window. Customers arrive at minutes 1, 2 and 3 with service times of 3, 1 and 1 minutes, and the server is free at minute 0. For how many of the ten minutes is the server idle?

The same 5 appears by counting the two gaps directly: one minute elapses before the first arrival and four minutes elapse after the last departure at minute 6. Nobody ever waits in this run, which is why the three service times stack end to end and the server is continuously occupied from minute 1 to minute 6, and that is worth checking explicitly since a model that never has a queue is not a model of a busy desk.

questions.topic: Utilisation of a single service point
questions.learningObjective: compute utilisation from an arrival rate and a mean service time
questions.stem: Customers arrive at a single service point at the rate of 12 per hour, and one customer occupies that point for 4 minutes on average. What is the utilisation of that service point?
questions.explanation: An hour holds 60 minutes and each customer takes 4 of them, so the point can serve 15 customers an hour and the utilisation is 12 divided by 15, which is 0.8. The same number comes from the workload side: 12 customers at 4 minutes each is 48 minutes of occupied time out of the 60 available, and 48 over 60 is again 0.8. The figure is worth having because it says whether the point can keep up at all: below one the queue can drain, at exactly one the point is permanently on the edge with no spare capacity, and above one the queue grows without bound however long the run is allowed to continue.
questions.hint: Turn the mean service time into a number of customers served per hour, then divide the arrival rate by it.

questions.stem: Customers arrive at a single service point at 14 per hour and are served there at 10 per hour. The queue is empty at 9 in the morning. How many customers are in the system at 3 in the afternoon?
questions.explanation: Six hours pass between 9 and 3, and in that time 14 times 6, which is 84, customers arrive while 10 times 6, which is 60, are served, leaving 84 minus 60, or 24, in the system. The same 24 falls out of the gap between the two rates: 4 more customers arrive than leave every hour, and 4 over 6 hours is 24. The number is the reason a utilisation model is worth building, because a gap of this size does not stay at 24, it adds 4 more every hour after that for as long as the rates hold, and that is the arithmetic a decision to add a second service point is really resting on.

questions.stem: Three single-server service points are on offer. Point one takes 9 customers per hour and serves 12, point two takes 14 and serves 12, and point three takes 12 and serves 12. Which point's queue cannot settle to a steady length?

options.text: Point two, because 14 arriving against 12 served makes the backlog grow by 2 every hour
Point three, because equal arrival and service rates leave the queue stuck at its starting length
options.misconception: reads equal rates as a frozen queue rather than a boundary case

options.text: Point one, because 9 arriving against 12 served empties the queue and then overfills it
options.misconception: believes a server faster than the arrivals will eventually overfill the queue

options.text: None of them, because a queue settles whenever the server is never fully occupied
options.misconception: assumes a lightly used server guarantees a steady queue

Point three sits exactly on the boundary, which is stable in the arithmetic sense but leaves no spare capacity at all, so a small rise in arrivals or a small fall in service tips it into growth. Point one is comfortably stable, and the last option states the condition wrongly, since a server that is never fully busy is precisely the case in which no queue can build at all.

questions.topic: Which parameter the output leans on
questions.learningObjective: identify the parameter a model is most sensitive to
questions.stem: A model predicts an expected wait as 200 minutes plus 2.5 minutes for each of 30 cases. Which pairing names the parameter the output is most sensitive to, and what that implies about where to spend effort?

options.text: The 200-minute base, because a 10 percent change to it moves the output further than the same change to either other
The 30-case volume, because a 10 percent change to it moves the output further than the same change to either other
options.misconception: assumes the largest input must be the most influential parameter

options.text: The 2.5-minute rate, because a 10 percent change to it moves the output further than the same change to either other
options.misconception: assumes the coefficient carrying a unit must be the most influential

options.text: All three equally, because each is a separate addend and separate addends always weigh the same
options.misconception: believes separate terms in a sum contribute equally to the result

questions.explanation: The output is 275, and raising the base to 220 gives 295, a move of 7.27 percent, while raising the rate to 2.75 gives 282.5 and raising the volume to 33 gives 282.5, both moves of 2.73 percent, so the base is roughly two and a half times as influential as either of the others. The reason is positional rather than dimensional: a large fixed addend contributes a large share of the total and therefore a large share of any change in it, while the two variable terms are small contributors no matter how precisely they are estimated. That is why effort spent sharpening the 2.5 buys so little here, and why the useful question is which parameter the arithmetic makes the answer depend on, not which one is hardest to measure.
questions.hint: Change each parameter by 10 percent in turn and compare how far the output moves each time.
