questions.topic: The largest movement from an equal-sized change
questions.learningObjective: compute the largest percentage change in an output under equal perturbations
questions.stem: Consider a model predicting an expected wait as 200 minutes plus 2.5 minutes for each of 30 cases, which gives 275 minutes. Raising each of the three parameters by 10 percent in turn with the others held fixed, the largest movement in the output comes from the 200-minute base. By what percentage does the output move when that base is raised by 10 percent?
questions.explanation: Raising the base to 220 gives 220 plus 75, which is 295, and 295 minus 275 is 20 against a starting value of 275, so 20 over 275 is 7.27 percent. The other two perturbations are much weaker: raising the rate to 2.75 gives 282.5 and raising the volume to 33 gives 282.5, each a change of 7.5, or 2.73 percent. Sensitivity is a property of where a parameter sits in the arithmetic rather than of how precisely it has been measured, which is why a big fixed term dominates two small variable ones and why a team can spend a great deal of care estimating the 2.5 and gain almost nothing for it.
questions.hint: Recompute the output with the base changed, subtract the original, then divide by the original.

questions.topic: Elasticity of a wait with respect to case volume
questions.learningObjective: compute an elasticity from a model and check it by finite difference
questions.stem: Elasticity measures how much an output responds to a change in one of its inputs. For a model predicting an expected wait as 200 minutes plus 2.5 minutes for each case, what is the elasticity of the output with respect to the number of cases, at 30 cases and an output of 275 minutes?

That gives 75 over 275, which is 0.2727. The figure checks out by finite difference: 30.1 cases give 275.25 while 30 give 275, so a rise of about 0.09 percent in the output accompanies a rise of about 0.33 percent in cases, and the ratio is again 0.2727. Sitting below one, the number says the fixed part of the model is indifferent to how busy the desk gets, which is why attacking that fixed part is the first move when waits are too long.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: One rate hiding a group that is failing
questions.learningObjective: explain what an overall rate conceals about a subgroup
questions.stem: A model scores 82 percent correct over a thousand cases. Inside that figure, one group of 100 scores 60 percent while the other 900 score about 84 percent. What does the single headline number conceal?

options.text: That one group is being judged far more badly than the rest, and the overall rate averages that away
Nothing, because 82 percent is the exact average of the two group rates and so is complete

questions.topic: An error wider than the gap a rule turns on
questions.learningObjective: recognise when a model's error exceeds a decision threshold
questions.stem: A model forecasts weekly demand and a rule places a reorder whenever the forecast is 3 units below stock. The model's typical error is 4 units. What follows from those two numbers together?

options.text: The error is wider than the gap the rule turns on, so the rule can fire on a shortfall that is not there
Nothing, because an error of 4 units is small beside a demand measured in hundreds of units
options.misconception: judges an error against the size of the quantity rather than the gap

options.text: Only that the forecast should be rounded, since rounding to the nearest unit removes most of the 4
options.misconception: believes a precision fix addresses an error larger than a threshold

options.text: That the rule is sound, since a forecast with any error at all beats having no forecast at all
options.misconception: treats beating nothing as sufficient justification for a rule

questions.explanation: The gap the rule turns on is 3 units and the uncertainty in the forecast is 4, so the model's noise is wider than the signal the rule is trying to detect, and a forecast that is 3 units short may be short by 3, by 7 or by nothing at all. A rule built on a threshold narrower than the model's own error cannot tell a real shortfall from an unlucky forecast, which is why its firings are not evidence about stock. The size of the quantity is beside the point, as the second option has it: a demand of a thousand does not make a 4-unit error into a small one, because the rule's decision lives entirely inside that 4. The repairs are a wider threshold, a better model, or a rule that acts on the expected cost of being wrong rather than on a single crossing.

questions.topic: Why a mostly-right rule still wastes money
questions.learningObjective: explain the risk of a threshold rule inside the model's own error
questions.stem: A reorder rule fires when a forecast shows a shortfall of 3 units or more, and the forecast's typical error is 4 units. Explain how a rule like this can be right most weeks and still place orders that were not needed, and name the figure that measures how often that happens.

answer.exemplar: The rule needs to see a gap of 3 units, but the forecast it reads is uncertain by 4, so the crossing it detects is often the model's own noise rather than a real shortfall; a forecast 3 units short may be 3 short, 7 short or not short at all, and the rule cannot tell those apart. Being right most weeks is compatible with this, because the weeks it is right on are the ones where the real shortfall and the error happened to point the same way. The figure that measures it is the count, or rate, of firings where no real shortfall was present, taken over all firings and not over all weeks, and it is the number a decision-maker should look at before trusting the rule.

questions.explanation: A threshold rule converts a continuous forecast into a yes-or-no action, and the conversion is only trustworthy when the thing being thresholded is measured more precisely than the distance to the threshold. Here it is not: the forecast is uncertain by 4 units while the rule needs a 3-unit gap, so a large share of firings are the forecast's own error crossing the line rather than a real shortage. A rule can be right on most of its firings and still be badly matched to the decision, because the firings that are wrong are concentrated where the forecast happened to be high, and those are precisely the cases where stock was adequate. The figure to compute is the number of firings with no real shortfall behind them, divided by all firings, since that is the rate at which the rule spends money for nothing, and it belongs beside any accuracy figure quoted for the model.
questions.hint: Ask how wide the forecast's uncertainty is against how wide the gap the rule needs, and what proportion of firings had nothing real behind them.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reading a projected value against the last real one
questions.learningObjective: identify the unsupported share of a projected value
questions.stem: A straight line is fitted to four readings at x = 1, 2, 3 and 4 with values 2.1, 4.3, 6.2 and 8.4, giving a slope of 2.08 and an intercept of 0.05. Used at x = 6 the line returns 12.53, while the largest value anyone observed was 8.4 at x = 4. What does the gap between those two figures show?

options.text: That 4.13 of the answer was produced with no reading anywhere near x = 6 to hold the line in place
That the slope of 2.08 is too low, since the last two readings rose by 2.2 a step and the fit missed that
options.misconception: criticises a least-squares fit for not matching the final step exactly

options.text: That the fit should be repeated on the same four points, since a second pass always improves a slope
options.misconception: believes refitting the same data can produce a different answer

options.text: That the readings are irregular, since 2.1, 4.3, 6.2 and 8.4 do not rise by an equal amount
options.misconception: treats a perfectly good linear pattern as evidence of bad data

questions.explanation: The projected value of 12.53 sits 4.13 above the largest observed value of 8.4, and every one of those 4.13 units was produced by the fitted slope carrying the line out into a region where nothing constrains it, since the four readings all lie at or below x = 4. A third of the answer is therefore faith rather than evidence, and the size of that share is the honest way to report a projection. The second option picks up a real feature of the data, the last step rising by 2.2, and treats it as a defect; least squares deliberately does not match the last step, because a fit that chased every local rise would be worse everywhere else, so 2.08 is the correct summary of all four points rather than a mistake in them.
questions.hint: Subtract the largest observed value from the projected one, and ask which readings could have influenced that difference.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a least-squares fit actually guarantees
questions.learningObjective: state the guarantee a least-squares fit makes and its limit
questions.stem: Explain what a least-squares fit guarantees about the data it was given, and say why that guarantee says nothing at all about a value beyond the largest one that was observed.

answer.exemplar: The guarantee is about the data that were supplied: among all straight lines through the points, the fitted one leaves the smallest possible total squared miss, and it does so by trading a miss on one point against a miss on another rather than by hitting any of them. That is a statement about the observed range only, because the fit has never seen a value above the largest one given to it, so nothing in the procedure tests what the line does out there. Read beyond the data the guarantee stops at the boundary, and the line continues only because the model form says it does, not because any reading supports it. A complete answer therefore names the guarantee as minimal squared error on the observed range, and the limit as the edge of that range.

questions.explanation: Least squares minimises one particular thing and nothing else: the total of the squared differences between the fitted line and the points that were handed to it, and it will deliberately miss several points rather than hit the rest exactly. That is a real guarantee, and a useful one, but its scope is precisely the sample it was computed from, because the procedure has no way of being wrong about a point it was never shown. A value past the largest observation is a different kind of statement altogether, resting on the assumption that the relationship keeps the shape the fit gave it, and that assumption was never examined by anything the fit did. This is why a fitted line can be exactly right in the middle of its range and have no standing at all two units past its end, and why a projection should always be published with the last observed value beside it so the reader can see how much of it is evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity the fitting procedure minimises, and over which points it does so.
